newsitem.title: UK: BA bid for Liberte stirs some market fears.
newsitem.headline: BA bid for Liberte stirs some market fears.

text.p: British Airways Plc could be throwing good money after bad if it succeeds in buying insolvent French airline Air Liberte while its TAT subsidiary is still losing money, but analysts said BA could yet prove them wrong.

"I am in little doubt that they will do a reasonable financial deal but whether or not they can turn it (Air Liberte) round in a short space of time is debatable," said Mike Powell of NatWest Markets. "I remain to be convinced," he said.
BA has offered only 25 million francs to buy Air Liberte from its court administrator and believes it can make the airline profitable by running it in tandem with TAT.
This would give the British group critical mass in the French domestic market, it hopes.

Analysts say Air Liberte might go on losing money under BA's control for some time to come but that has been factored into the price BA is prepared to pay for it. BA has emphasised that its bid is only valid until the end of the month.

Air Liberte lost 650 million francs in the first nine months of 1996. But it controls about a quarter of all runway slots at Paris Orly airport and there is some belief that the air fare war which has plagued the domestic market will end.

Analysts say Air France, which dominates the local market with its Air France Europe arm, cannot go on discounting fares because of the terms set by the European Commission for its state-subsidised rescue plan.

"That aid is conditional. They will not be able to continue pumping money to finance losses in this (domestic) market and that will give BA an opportunity," said Stephen Clapham, industry analyst at Robert Fleming.
"The French domestic market is a large market with a weak dominant player. It is perfectly logical for BA to attack that market and whichever way they do it it will be successful."
BA says Air Liberte carried 2.6 million passengers in 1995/1996, operates 15 aircraft and has about 12 percent of the French domestic market from Orly.
In comparison TAT operates 26 aircraft, carried 1.8 million passengers last year and has a 10 percent share of the domestic market from Orly.
TAT chairman Marc Rochet, who would also manage Air Liberte if the bid is successful, said on Monday that he expects TAT to swing into profit with or without an Air Liberte merger.
BA chief executive Bob Ayling said in August he expected TAT would show another loss for the year to end-March 1997 but expects to see it coming into profit by next year.

BA routinely declines to detail TAT's losses since but said last year combined losses from TAT and German affiliate Deutsche BA together fell to 68 million stg last year, down from a 93 million stg deficit in 1994/1995.
Analysts estimate that about two-thirds of those losses were attributable to TAT.
